paras: The manhunt for Harry Thomas was an armed search in Clarke County, Virginia, in early September 1903 for a Black man accused of taking part in an assault on Capt. James M. Haymaker, a Winchester councilman and night watchman. On September 5 a party of armed men led by Winchester's police chief found Thomas in a corn field near the Shenandoah River, but he escaped, and a further search by a constable and deputized citizens also failed. Thomas was caught in Pennsylvania months later and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary in February 1904.

According to a Winchester dispatch to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, Haymaker was "murderously assaulted" shortly after 11 p.m. on August 27 by "two drunken negro brutes, Shack Johnson and Henry Thompson" while on duty as a special policeman and watchman at Baker and Company's warehouse. That report credited Charles Brown, "a colored man," with scaring the attackers off, while the Martinsburg Herald said Johnson knocked the watchman down after being told to stop cursing. Johnson was caught that night, and police kept an armed crowd from lynching him.

The second man was first reported to have escaped on a freight train and been arrested, and the Martinsburg Herald named him as possibly "Harry Wiltshire, of Atlanta," jailed in Maryland for stealing a ride. On the night of Monday, August 31, searching parties of young white men in Winchester, acting on a rumor that the accomplice was hiding at the house of Mollie Smith, a Black woman, broke in her door and fired revolvers inside. The Alexandria Gazette wrote that had he been found "he would undoubtedly have been lynched on the spot"; the men arrested on Smith's complaint were discharged.

On September 5 Chief S. A. Seabright and Officers McIntosh and Taylor led "a party of armed men" to capture Thomas, whom they located in a corn field near the Shenandoah River in Clarke County. The Times-Dispatch reported that "it is believed he saw the men approaching and escaped." Mayor Graichen of Winchester then offered a $50 reward for his arrest.

The Clarke Courier's correspondent at Bowles wrote of "great excitement in the neighborhood for the past ten days" over the search; Thomas's wife came from there and had returned to her mother's home. The local constable and a number of deputized citizens joined the hunt, and Thomas was seen several times but not captured and was believed to have left the county. No report describes shots fired at Thomas or any injury during the search.

On September 21 Johnson was indicted by a special grand jury, tried and sentenced the same day to nine years and six months, and Thomas, still at large, was indicted as well. In January 1904 Thomas was brought back to Winchester from Pennsylvania, where, according to the Alexandria Gazette, he admitted his identity although no one there could have identified him, and confessed his part in the assault. On February 18, 1904, the Corporation Court sentenced him to seven years in the penitentiary.

The case appeared only in white newspapers, chiefly the Richmond Times-Dispatch through Winchester specials, the Martinsburg Herald and the Clarke Courier of Berryville, with briefs elsewhere. The Clarke Courier reprinted the Times-Dispatch account of the assault nearly word for word. The manhunt itself ran under the headlines "PURSUIT OF CRIMINAL" and "OFFERS REWARD," and every report described Thomas as "the negro who assaulted" Haymaker, stating the accusation as fact.

Coverage of the crowd violence was more critical: the attack on Smith's house ran as "WOULD-BE LYNCHERS" in the Alexandria Gazette and "MOB AT WINCHESTER" with the subhead "Hot headed Young Men Create a Serious Disturbance" in the Martinsburg Herald. The Virginia Gazette headed its report of Johnson's same-day indictment, trial and sentence "Speedy Justice." No Black-press coverage of the assault, the search or the trials was found.

Reports gave the hunted man's name as "Henry Thompson," "Henry Thomas," "Harry Johnson" and, in the later and court reports, "Harry Thomas." Early accounts of his arrest on a freight train or in Maryland conflict with the September search and with his capture in Pennsylvania months later.

Reports of the attack on Mollie Smith's house ran under 'WOULD-BE LYNCHERS' and 'MOB AT WINCHESTER. Hot headed Young Men Create a Serious Disturbance', while calling Johnson 'a negro tough'.
The Virginia Gazette headed Johnson's same-day indictment, trial and sentence 'Speedy Justice.'
